topic: Healthcare costs push millions to poverty
headline_marked: [[1.08 crore Bangladeshis pushed into poverty]] by out-of-pocket medical bills in 2022: Study
headline: 1.08 crore Bangladeshis pushed into poverty by out-of-pocket medical bills in 2022: Study
summary: Over 1.08 crore Bangladeshis, 6.4% of the population, were pushed below the poverty line in 2022 by out-of-pocket healthcare costs, a new study finds. This is nearly double the 2005 figure, despite the national poverty rate halving.
details: A recent government study reveals that over 1.08 crore Bangladeshis, or 6.4 percent of the population, were pushed below the poverty line in 2022 due to out-of-pocket (OOP) healthcare expenditure. This figure is almost double the 56 lakh people affected in 2005.

The rise in impoverishing healthcare costs occurred even as the national poverty rate more than halved, from 40 percent in 2005 to 18.7 percent in 2022. The share of the population facing financial hardship due to healthcare spending also significantly increased from 28.2 percent in 2005 to 41.7 percent in 2022.

OOP payments are direct household expenses for healthcare, including medicines, diagnostic tests, and treatment, not covered by the government or other sources. A person faces financial hardship when OOP payments exceed 40 percent of their disposable income after basic needs are met.

The study, titled "Financial Risk Associated with Out-of-Pocket Healthcare Payments and Benefit Incidence in Bangladesh," was conducted by the Health Economics Unit (HEU) with support from the WHO and the Swedish Embassy. Its findings were presented in Dhaka.

The incidence of catastrophic health expenditure (CHE), where OOP payments exceed 10 percent of total household consumption, climbed sharply from 12.5 percent in 2005 to 32.1 percent in 2022. The WHO has since replaced CHE with financial hardship as a more accurate indicator.

Average monthly household OOP payments, adjusted for inflation, rose from Tk 1,241 in 2005 to Tk 3,238 in 2022. Concurrently, the proportion of households reporting any OOP payment surged from 52.5 percent to 92.7 percent during the same period.

Medicines, diagnostic tests, hospitalisation, and consultation fees were identified as major contributors to these expenses. The study also noted a growing reliance on pharmacies for outpatient care, with their share increasing from 32.5 percent in 2016 to 55.4 percent in 2022.

The poorest households were disproportionately affected, with 90.8 percent in the lowest consumption quintile facing financial hardship, compared to 13.6 percent in the richest. Rural populations also bore a greater burden, with 47.9 percent facing hardship versus 28.2 percent in urban areas.

Barishal division experienced a significant reversal, moving from the lowest rate of financial hardship in 2005 (22.5 percent) to the highest in 2022 (59.1 percent). This highlights regional disparities in healthcare access and affordability.

Public facilities remain the primary provider of inpatient care, but their share decreased from 61.3 percent in 2016 to 56 percent in 2022, while private sector involvement grew. Concerns were also raised about the distribution of public healthcare benefits, which no longer clearly favored poorer households.

To mitigate financial hardship, the study recommends increasing public financing, improving spending efficiency and equity, and restoring pro-poor distribution of public healthcare benefits. It also calls for ensuring free and reliable access to essential medicines and diagnostics, and affordable care for chronic conditions.

headline_marked: Bangladesh assures [[sufficient supplies]] for Ramadan, no edible oil price hike planned
headline: Bangladesh assures sufficient supplies for Ramadan, no edible oil price hike planned
summary: The Commerce Minister stated that adequate essential commodities are in the import pipeline to meet demand during Ramadan. He also confirmed no immediate plans to increase edible oil prices.
details: Bangladesh is poised to have sufficient supplies of essential commodities for the upcoming Ramadan, according to Commerce Minister Khandakar Abdul Muktadir. He assured that ample goods, including edible oil, chickpeas, pulses, and sugar, are already in the import pipeline to meet anticipated demand.

The minister explicitly stated that the government has no immediate plans to raise the prices of edible oil. While chickpea prices have seen a slight increase internationally, discussions are ongoing with importers to manage the situation. The government remains vigilant in ensuring uninterrupted supply and market stability.

Imports of key Ramadan commodities have shown a year-on-year increase. Edible oil imports rose to 8.23 lakh tonnes, sugar to 6.87 lakh tonnes, chickpeas to 82,000 tonnes, red lentils to 1.22 lakh tonnes, and dates to 11,000 tonnes. Import commitments, indicated by Letters of Credit (LCs) openings, also saw increases for several items.

Despite improved import volumes, the minister acknowledged that international commodity prices and shipping freight rates remain critical factors influencing import costs and domestic market prices. The Bangladesh Trade and Tariff Commission (BTTC) is closely monitoring global market trends and import costs.

In parallel, Bangladesh has initiated formal negotiations for a Free Trade Agreement (FTA) with Malaysia, with the aim to conclude by December 2027. Discussions are also underway with other key trading partners, including the UAE, Indonesia, Oman, New Zealand, and the EU, to secure preferential trade benefits post-LDC graduation.
